books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883)
Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
William Graham Sumner, “The Forgotten Man,” in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883):

“The type and formula of most schemes of philanthropy or humanitarianism is this: A and B put their heads together to decide what C shall be made to do for D. The radical vice of all these schemes, from a sociological point of view, is that C is not allowed a voice in the matter, and his position, character, and interests, as well as the ultimate effects on society through C’s interests, are entirely overlooked. I call C the Forgotten Man.”

Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889:

“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.”
stimulus.source_note: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883); Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889. Both quotations are exact.

stem: According to Sumner, who is the Forgotten Man?

options.text: The rich industrialist who funds the scheme himself
options.misconception: Sumner calls C the Forgotten Man, and C is the one made to pay, not the rich funder.

options.text: The worker made to pay for schemes he never chose
The government official who writes the new law
options.misconception: A and B design the scheme; C, the Forgotten Man, is the one made to pay for it.

options.text: The poor man who receives the aid money himself
options.misconception: D receives the aid; C is the Forgotten Man who pays for it.

rationales.A: C is the one made to pay, not the rich man funding the scheme.
rationales.B: C is made to do something for D, with no voice in the matter.
rationales.C: A and B design the scheme; C is the one made to pay for it.
rationales.D: D receives the aid; C is the Forgotten Man who pays for it.
rationales.general:
Follow the letters in Sumner's formula.
1. A and B plan a scheme to help D, the person in need.
2. C is the one made to pay for it, with no voice in the matter.
3. Sumner calls C the Forgotten Man, because reformers overlook him.
4. The Forgotten Man is the ordinary worker who pays, not the giver or the receiver.
Remember: a formula's letters name the roles, so track each letter.
